description: Unity's behaviours on three.js, with scenes written in TSX and no React.
rules: A game on SceNoCo: three.js scenes written in TSX — there is no React — and Unity's model of behaviours, named `Behaviour`. Everything not described here is plain three.js, TypeScript, DOM and CSS: write what you know. Every SceNoCo signature is in `node_modules/@scenoco-three/core/API.md` — read it instead of the package's source. Three's classes import from `three`, SceNoCo's (`Behaviour`, `play`, `prefab`, `ref`, `Input`, `Time`, …) from `@scenoco-three/core`.

**Checking it.** `scenoco check src`, from `@scenoco-three/tools`, checks that every `.tsx` file only declares; `tsc` checks the rest. The game's rules are tested in Vitest, in Node or jsdom, with no canvas: `const game = simulate(Main)` builds the scene and runs nothing until the test steps it — `game.press(KeyCode.Space)`, `game.step(60)`, `expect(game.until(() => findObjectOfType(GameState)!.phase === 'over')).toBe(true)`, then `game.dispose()`. Frames have a fixed `dt`, so the answer is the same every run. In development the page drives the running game from `window.__scenoco` (`__scenoco.help()` lists it): hold and step its clock, press keys, click, swipe, read behaviours by class. Evaluate in the page with any browser tool — `async () => { await __scenoco.ready(); await __scenoco.press('Space'); return __scenoco.until("GameState.phase === 'over'") }` — then take its screenshot; a Playwright test makes the same calls through `page.evaluate`. A tool that can only open an address, read the console and take a screenshot puts the same calls in the address, driving the game to the moment it needs to see: `/?drive=press('Space');until(GameState.phase == 'over');read(count(Brick))` logs one console line per call and holds the clock there for the screenshot (`#` is `%23` in an address). It reads data, not code — behaviours' fields and getters, `#node`s, `Time`, `count`/`find`/`findAll(Type)` — so a check it can't say goes in the game: a getter (`get bricksLeft()`), or a starting point the game reads itself (`/?level=3&drive=…`, read in `main.ts`). A behaviour that throws is logged once and the game goes on, as in Unity — read the console. Log each change of the game's state with `console.info` — `phase: playing`, `score: 3` — so the console alone shows the rules working.

**Scenes.** A `.tsx` file is a scene or a prefab, and it only declares — no hooks, loops, branches or handlers; `scenoco check` points at them. An object made from data with `new` — a font, a curve — is a constant above the scene function: `const font = new Font(json)`. A tag is a three.js class you import: `<BoxGeometry args={[1, 2, 3]} />` is `new BoxGeometry(1, 2, 3)`, and attributes are its properties, R3F-style — `position={[0, 1, 0]}`, `color="#ff8800"`, `scale={2}`, `shadow-mapSize={[1024, 1024]}`. A child node is added to its parent; a geometry or material fills `geometry` / `material`; anything else names the property it fills: `<Fog attach="fog" args={['#000000', 5, 30]} />`, `<Color attach="background" args={['#000000']} />`. A node with `attach` is both added and assigned: `<Object3D attach="target" position={[0, -1, 0]} />` inside a `DirectionalLight` is where it shines, and moves with it.

**Behaviours.** What lives in the scene and changes over time — moves, reacts, animates — is Unity's MonoBehaviour: `class X extends Behaviour<Mesh>` in a `.ts` file, with the same hooks in camelCase (awake, onEnable, start, fixedUpdate, update(dt), lateUpdate, onDisable, onDestroy; onValidate after the editor changed a field or moved a node it holds, to redo what start built). `this.node` is the three.js object it is on. Public fields are its settings, set as attributes when it is attached as a TSX child of its node: `<Mesh><Spinner speed={2} /></Mesh>`.

**Links.** A typed ref made in the scene function links two objects: `const paddle = ref<Group>()`, `<Group ref={paddle}>`, `<Follow target={paddle} />` — the field holds the object itself, `target: Group | null = null`. A behaviour's tag takes `ref` too, linking that component: `<Rigidbody2D ref={wheel} />`, `<WheelJoint2D connectedBody={wheel} />`. In code, behaviours find each other as in Unity — `getComponent(T)`, `getComponentInChildren(T)`, `findObjectOfType(T)`, `findObjectsOfType(T)` — and can talk through `Event<T>` fields and `this.listen(event, fn)`. Unity's tags are empty behaviours — `class Enemy extends Behaviour {}`, `<Enemy />` on the node: `other.getComponent(Enemy)` is `CompareTag`, `findObjectsOfType(Enemy)` is `FindGameObjectsWithTag`.

**Prefabs.** A prefab is made with `prefab()` around a function returning TSX with one root: `export const Coin = prefab(() => <Mesh>…</Mesh>)`. Its tag places and names that root as a Unity instance's Transform does — `<Coin position={[2, 0, 0]} name="bonus" />` — so a prefab never declares `position`, `rotation`, `scale` or `name` itself. Only a prefab is instantiated — `instantiate(Coin, { position })` builds a fresh one each call — or taken by a field, as Unity's inspector does: `shot: Prefab | null = null`, `<Gun shot={Bullet} />`. A function not wrapped is a plain TSX component, reused markup whose tag is its props: `<Arena ballSpeed={16} />`. Anything placed more than once — a wall, a tree, a crate, static or not — is a prefab, with what differs as its props: `export const Wall = prefab(({ width = 1 }) => …)`, `<Wall position={[-9, 0, 0]} width={0.5} />`. The editor edits a prefab once for every copy and each copy's props on its tag; inside a plain component placed twice it edits nothing, since one edit there would change every use. A scene is a plain function returning `<Scene>`: `SceneManager.load(Level2)`; `dontDestroyOnLoad(this)` keeps a node across loads.

**Levels are the user's to edit.** What a designer arranges — a level, a puzzle, a wave, where the pickups are — is one element per object in a scene, `<Brick position={[2.55, -1, 0]} hits={2} />`, never a string map, an array or a loop: the editor moves them and edits their props, and the file says what it did. A prefab's props show in the editor at their defaults. Give such objects help for placing them by hand, as behaviours: snap to a grid in `onValidate` — with a `snap = true` field to turn it off — clamp a value, keep to a path.

**Assets.** A glTF model is `const hero = sharedModel('/hero.glb')`, awaited with `await loadAssets(hero)` in `main.ts`, then `instantiate(hero, { parent: this.node })`; its clips play through an `Animator` (`addComponent(Animator)`, `animator.crossFade('Run', 0.1)`). A texture is `sharedTexture(url)`: one per URL, shared by every material that uses it.

**Time.** `destroy(node)` is deferred to the end of the frame, as in Unity. Coroutines are Unity's: `this.startCoroutine(this.spawnWaves())` runs a generator method that yields `new WaitForSeconds(2)`, `new WaitUntil(() => …)` or `null` (a frame). `Time.timeScale = 0` pauses: `update` keeps running with `dt` 0, while fixedUpdate, physics and `WaitForSeconds` stop — timing done with setTimeout or Date.now does not pause with it.

**Input and UI.** UI is HTML and CSS in `index.html`, read and written with DOM APIs. A `<button data-button="Pause">` reads like a key: `Input.getButtonDown('Pause')`. Give every control one, labelled — `<button data-button="Jump">Jump</button>` — beside its key: a phone has no keys, and a browser tool that cannot click the canvas or press keys can still press a button. Keys, axes and the pointer are Unity's: `Input.getKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)`, `Input.getAxis('Horizontal')`, `Input.getMouseButtonDown(MouseButton.Left)`, `Input.pointer`. A gamepad is too: its left stick and d-pad move the same axes, its buttons are `KeyCode.JoystickButton0…` and Unity's named buttons (A is `Fire1`/`Submit`), and `Input.getJoystickNames()` says whether one is there. A stick drawn on the page drives an axis with `Input.setAxis('Horizontal', x)`, and `null` when let go.

**Space.** three.js is right-handed — x right, y up, z towards the viewer — where Unity is left-handed, z away; a camera looks down its own -z. Rotations are radians — `rotation={[-Math.PI / 2, 0, 0]}` lays a plane flat — where Unity's inspector shows degrees; 2D physics angles are degrees, as Unity's are.

**Physics** is a package: `npm install @scenoco-three/rapier` (3D) or `@scenoco-three/box2d` (2D). Bodies and colliders are Unity's components — `<Rigidbody />` plus a collider on the same element, and colliders on elements under it too, one compound body; a collider alone is static and still follows its node — and contacts arrive as `onCollisionEnter(collision)` / `onTriggerEnter(other)`. Unity's `Physics.raycast`, `CharacterController` and joints are there as Unity has them; everything else is Rapier's own API, used directly: `Physics.world`, `rb.rapierBody`, `collider.rapierCollider`. With rapier, `main.ts` starts with `await initRapier();`. box2d is the same in 2D, in the XY plane: `Rigidbody2D`, `BoxCollider2D`, `Physics2D.raycast`, Unity's nine 2D joints, and `Physics2D.world` and `rb.planckBody` for planck's own.

**More packages**, each in Unity's shape, each with its README in `node_modules/@scenoco-three/<name>/`: `particles` (`ParticleSystem`), `audio` (`AudioSource`), `splines` (`SplineContainer`, `SplineMesh`, `SplineAnimate`: tracks, rails, roads) and `terrain` (`Terrain`, `TerrainData`). Install one before writing your own.

**Starting.** `main.ts` runs `const game = play(Main);`. The scene's first visible camera draws it, so a scene puts its camera in, as in Unity — one without draws nothing; `visible = false` on it hands over to the next, as Unity's `camera.enabled` does. An `OrthographicCamera` keeps its height and widens with the screen. `play(Main, { autoCamera: false })` leaves cameras to you: set `game.camera` and size it. `game.renderer` is three's WebGLRenderer, configured as three.js documents it — `game.renderer.shadowMap.enabled = true`. Inside a React app the game is one element of the page: `play(Main, { container })` in an effect, `game.dispose()` in its cleanup, and `scenoco({ include: 'src/game/**' })` beside `react({ exclude: /src\/game\// })` in `vite.config.ts` keeps the app's own TSX React's.

From Unity: gameObject/transform → `this.node` · transform.localPosition → `this.node.position` (three's position is in the parent's space) · transform.position → `this.node.getWorldPosition(v)` · Time.deltaTime → `update(dt)` or `Time.deltaTime` · GetComponent<T>() → `getComponent(T)` · FindObjectOfType<T>() → `findObjectOfType(T)` · Instantiate → `instantiate` · Destroy → `destroy` · Camera.main → `this.camera` · StartCoroutine → `this.startCoroutine` · `yield return new WaitForSeconds(1)` → `yield new WaitForSeconds(1)`
